A national bank for all states
Dissolution of the state militias

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the Supremacy Clause
questions.stem: A bee log asks how the Supremacy Clause resolves conflicts.

answer.exemplar: The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme, so conflicting state laws yield to valid federal statutes and the Constitution.

questions.explanation: Federal law prevails over conflicting state law. The wrong idea is that states may nullify federal statutes.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the amendment process

stimulus.body: The Constitution can be amended by proposal from two-thirds of both houses of Congress or a convention, followed by ratification by three-fourths of the states.

questions.stem: A hive record asks what fraction of states must ratify an amendment.

options.text: A simple majority of the states
Two-thirds of the states
Three-fourths of the states
Unanimous consent of all states

questions.explanation: Ratification requires three-fourths of states. The wrong options misstate the threshold.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the Sixth Amendment's protections
questions.stem: A beekeeper's log asks which amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial.

options.text: The Eighth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial
options.misconception: confuses punishment limits with trial rights

options.text: The Fifth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial
options.misconception: assigns Sixth Amendment content to the Fifth

options.text: The Seventh Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial
options.misconception: confuses civil jury with criminal trial

options.text: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial

questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees speedy, public trials. The wrong options borrow from other amendments.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of George Washington at the Convention
questions.stem: A hive log asks what role George Washington played at the Constitutional Convention.

options.text: He opposed the new Constitution entirely
He presided as president of the convention
He drafted the entire Constitution alone
He refused to attend the convention

questions.explanation: Washington presided over the Convention. The wrong options reverse or exaggerate his role.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the necessity of the Great Compromise
questions.stem: A bee log asks why the Great Compromise was necessary.

answer.exemplar: Without it, large and small states could not agree on representation, threatening the Convention's success and the union.

questions.explanation: The compromise resolved the representation dispute that threatened the Convention. The wrong idea is that states agreed easily.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the Anti-Federalist pen name Brutus
questions.stem: A hive record asks which pen name an Anti-Federalist writer used.

options.text: Cato
options.misconception: names a different Anti-Federalist pen name

options.text: Publius
Brutus
Pacificus
options.misconception: names a later Hamilton pen name

questions.explanation: Brutus was an Anti-Federalist pen name. Publius was Federalist. The wrong options confuse pen names.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the Elastic Clause's significance

stimulus.body: The Elastic Clause, or Necessary and Proper Clause, allows Congress to make laws required to execute its enumerated powers, expanding federal capacity beyond the explicit list.

questions.stem: A bee log asks what the Elastic Clause allows Congress to do.

options.text: Declare war unilaterally
Ignore the Constitution when convenient
Tax without any limits
Pass laws necessary to execute enumerated powers

questions.explanation: The Elastic Clause permits laws necessary to execute enumerated powers. The wrong options misstate its scope.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the judicial branch's review power
questions.stem: A hive diary asks which branch can declare laws unconstitutional.

options.text: The executive branch by veto
The judicial branch through judicial review
The legislative branch by repeal
The states by nullification

questions.explanation: Courts exercise judicial review. The wrong options confuse it with veto, repeal, or nullification.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Summarize the Bill of Rights' purpose

stimulus.body: The Bill of Rights comprises the first ten amendments, limiting federal power and protecting freedoms such as speech, religion, and due process, addressing Anti-Federalist concerns.

questions.stem: A bee log asks what the Bill of Rights primarily did.

options.text: Abolished state governments
Granted new powers to the federal government
Limited federal power and protected individual liberties
Established a national religion

questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights limits federal power and protects liberties. The wrong options reverse or exaggerate its purpose.
